title: Guidelines to Prevent Abuse of PIL (State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal)

content.overview: Abuse-control guidelines require courts to screen PIL for credentials, motive, substantial public injury, and absence of personal gain before full entertainment. Liberal standing is preserved for genuine claims; private, publicity, and political misuse are filtered, with costs where appropriate.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Petitioner credentials? (2) Genuine public injury? (3) Personal or political gain? (4) Adequate particulars? (5) Costs for clear abuse?
content.study:
Core rule: Access without screens invites docket capture by private and motivated litigation. Guidelines crystallise credential checks, bona fides, substantial public injury, and costs as the counterpart of liberal standing.

Typical screens: identity and interest of the petitioner; whether the injury is public and substantial; whether the petition seeks personal, commercial, or political advantage; whether facts are adequately pleaded; whether alternative remedies exist for private grievances.

Relationship to limits-and-costs: This topic focuses on the guideline framework associated with screening practice; the companion limits topic covers private-dispute filters and exemplary costs more broadly.

Current-law framing: Articles 32 and 226 plus judicial screening. Case entries retained; verification gate open — do not treat any guideline list as exhaustively verified without the evidence gate.

sections.heading: Why guidelines exist
sections.body: Liberal standing expanded access. Without screening, courts face private disputes, publicity petitions, and political instruments labelled as PIL. Guidelines protect genuine public-interest claims by filtering abuse early.

sections.heading: Credential and motive checks
sections.body: Courts examine who the petitioner is, what interest is disclosed, and whether the purpose is bona fide public redress rather than personal or collateral advantage.

sections.heading: Substantial public injury
sections.body: A vague recitation of public interest is not enough. The petition should show a real public or class injury capable of judicial redress under Articles 32 or 226.

sections.heading: Consequences of abuse
sections.body: Dismissal or refusal at the threshold, and costs including heavy or exemplary costs in serious misuse, deter repetition without closing the door on genuine claims.

sections.heading: Preserving genuine access
sections.body: Guidelines are not a return to strict personal standing. Bona fide representative claims for disadvantaged classes remain maintainable when public injury and good faith are shown.

examples.title: Publicity petition
examples.body: A petitioner with no connection to the subject matter seeks sweeping directions mainly for media attention. Credential and motive screens justify refusal.

examples.title: Genuine class injury
examples.body: A documented systemic denial of a statutory benefit to a remote class is pleaded with particulars and bona fides. Screening should not block the claim merely because standing is representative.

hypotheticals.question: Do abuse guidelines abolish PIL?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. They pair liberal access with screening so genuine claims proceed and misuse is filtered.

distinctions.title: Abuse guidelines vs general limits-and-costs
distinctions.left: Guidelines topic: structured screening themes (credentials, motive, public injury).
distinctions.right: Limits topic: broader private-dispute, busybody, alternative-remedy, and costs analysis.

misconceptions.trap: Any procedural irregularity means the PIL is abusive.
misconceptions.correction: Abuse turns on motive, private character, and want of public injury — not every formal defect.

questionsAndAnswers.answer: State the need for screens after liberal standing. Cover credentials, motive, substantial public injury, absence of personal gain, and costs. Stress preservation of genuine access.
